title: Mars can have blue sunsets
body: Mars is the Red Planet, but its sunsets can glow **blue near the Sun**. Fine dust in the thin atmosphere scatters blue light mostly in the Sun's direction, while other colors spread more widely. When sunlight takes a longer path through that dust at sunset, the difference becomes easier to see. NASA's rovers have photographed the effect from the surface.

A blue glow around the setting Sun

slides.heading: Dust sorts the colors
slides.text: The dust grains scatter different colors in different directions. Blue light stays more concentrated around the Sun, creating a bluish glow.

left.label: Daytime
left.text: Airborne dust often gives the Martian sky a reddish or butterscotch tint.

right.label: Sunset
right.text: The sky close to the Sun can look blue. The amount of dust affects how strong the color appears.

slides.heading: More than a pretty picture
slides.text: Sunset images help scientists study how high Martian dust reaches and look for dust or ice clouds.

slides.question: Why does the Martian sky near the setting Sun look blue?
options: Dust sends blue light mostly Sunward
Its thin air scatters light like Earth’s
Ice clouds reflect a blue glow
The Sun looks bluer from farther away
slides.explanation: Fine dust in the thin atmosphere scatters blue light mostly in the Sun’s direction, while other colours spread more widely. At sunset the longer path through dust makes it easier to see.

slides.heading: Mars or Earth?

items.text: The daytime sky is reddish or butterscotch
The sky near the setting Sun glows blue
Air molecules scatter blue across the whole sky
Fine dust does most of the scattering

slides.explanation: Earth’s air molecules scatter blue light everywhere; Mars’s fine dust sends blue light mostly toward the Sun, so its sunsets glow blue.
